read: full (main text pp. 1-6, references pp. 6-8, Appendix A.1-A.3 pp. 9-12; the judge-prompt tables, pp. 12-17, skimmed)
venue_now: arXiv 2404.18796v2, 1 May 2024 (p. 1 footer); the text shows no venue, and papers.json records 'arXiv only as of 2026-10'. The May entry (arXiv preprint) is correct.
what_it_is: A Cohere study of LLM-as-a-judge evaluation that proposes replacing a single large judge (GPT-4) with a Panel of LLm evaluators (PoLL): several judges from disjoint model families score each output independently, and a voting function pools the scores (pp. 1-2). The instantiated panel is Command R, Claude 3 Haiku and GPT-3.5, pooled by max voting for binary QA correctness and by averaging for 1-5 Chatbot Arena scores (p. 3). Across three settings and six datasets (single-hop KILT QA, multi-hop QA with ReAct agents, Chatbot Arena Hard), the panel agrees with human judgements more closely than the single GPT-4 judge wherever GPT-4 was a judge, shows less intra-model bias, and costs seven to eight times less (pp. 4-6).
domain: LLM evaluation methodology (LLM-as-a-judge) on open-domain question answering and open-ended chat (Chatbot Arena Hard)
size: Six datasets in three settings: KILT Natural Questions, TriviaQA and HotpotQA (single-hop); Bamboogle (125 questions) and HotpotQA (multi-hop); Chatbot Arena Hard (500 prompts) (pp. 2-3, p. 10). Judges: Command R, Claude 3 Haiku and GPT-3.5 (the panel) and GPT-4 (single). Evaluated models: Command R and R+, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, Claude 3 Haiku and Sonnet, Mistral Large and Medium (p. 3, Tables 5-7). Human annotations: NQ 688 (triple), TriviaQA 316 (single), HotpotQA single-hop 784 (triple), HotpotQA multi-hop 595 (single), Bamboogle 750 (single) (Table 8, p. 12).
source_of_items: existing datasets (KILT, Bamboogle, HotpotQA, Arena Hard); the judged outputs are generations of the evaluated models (pp. 3, 9-10)
has_gold_traces: no: QA items carry human-annotated reference answers used for reference-based judging (p. 3); no intermediate steps are judged
evaluation: LLM judge (single or panel), validated against human judgements: Cohen's kappa against human correctness labels for QA (p. 4), Pearson and Kendall correlation of model rankings with the Chatbot Arena leaderboard (p. 4), and each judge's accuracy deviation from human scores per evaluated model (p. 5)
human_validation: Cohere's internal professional annotators (novelists, copywriters, copy editors, journalists) judged whether the reference answer is semantically contained in a generated answer (p. 4, p. 11). NQ and single-hop HotpotQA were triple-annotated and pooled by majority vote; the other sets were singly annotated (p. 11, Table 8 p. 12). No inter-annotator agreement is reported. Chatbot Arena's crowd-sourced ranking is the ground truth for that setting (p. 3).

engtrace_use.sentence: Building upon the 'Panel of LLM' (PoLL) methodology (Verga et al., 2024), we construct an 'AI Tribunal' comprising three frontier reasoning models: GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025a), Claude Opus 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025b), and Gemini 3 (Google, 2025). (Section 3.3, L260-265)
engtrace_use.explanation: The element EngTrace borrowed is credited correctly: PoLL scores each output with several independent judges from different model families and pools their verdicts (pp. 2-3), and the Tribunal did the same with judges from three organisations. The characterisation is loose in three ways. (1) The method is the 'Panel of LLm evaluators' (p. 1), not the 'Panel of LLM'. (2) PoLL's defining claim is that a panel of smaller models can replace a single large judge (title 'Replacing Judges with Juries'; abstract p. 1: 'very large models are often unnecessary'), whereas the Tribunal is three frontier models, and it pools by median score and majority vote (May Eq. 1, L270-275, and the check that follows) rather than PoLL's max or average pooling (p. 3). (3) PoLL's evidence covers reference-based QA correctness and Chatbot Arena preferences (pp. 3-4), and its authors say applicability to 'math or reasoning evaluations' needs further work (p. 6), while the Tribunal audited template source code and generated instances against a multi-axis rubric (L266-269). 'Building upon' borrows PoLL's idea; none of PoLL's validation transfers to that use, and the revision should not imply that it does.

suggested_wording: A panel of three smaller judges from disjoint model families (PoLL; Verga et al., 2024) agreed with human correctness labels on open-domain QA more closely than a single GPT-4 judge, showed less intra-model bias and cost seven to eight times less, though its authors leave math and reasoning evaluation untested.
facts_to_cite: PoLL (Panel of LLm evaluators) scores an output with several judges from different model families and pools their scores with a voting function (pp. 1-2).
The instantiated panel is Command R, Claude 3 Haiku and GPT-3.5, pooled by max voting for binary QA judgements and by averaging for 1-5 Arena scores (p. 3).

Cohen's kappa against human correctness labels on KILT NQ, TriviaQA and HotpotQA: PoLL 0.763, 0.906 and 0.867; GPT-4 0.627, 0.841 and 0.830; exact match 0.651, 0.827 and 0.662 (Table 1, p. 4). Haiku alone reaches 0.873 on HotpotQA.
Against the Chatbot Arena leaderboard, PoLL's model ranking has Pearson 0.917 and Kendall tau 0.778, against GPT-4's 0.817 and 0.667 (Table 2, p. 4).
GPT-4's agreement as a judge on NQ moves from kappa 0.518 (zero-shot) to 0.725 (an instruction not to 'overthink') with prompt changes (Table 3, p. 5).

Intra-model bias: each evaluated model receives its largest positive deviation from human scores when it is judged by itself, and the GPT-4 judge ranks a GPT-4 variant second rather than fourth (p. 5).
On multi-hop QA, PoLL's deviations from human scores have the smallest spread (standard deviation 2.2, against 6.1 for GPT-3.5) (p. 5).
The panel costs seven to eight times less than a single GPT-4 Turbo judge (p. 6).
Limits stated by the authors: three settings and few judges and panel compositions; applicability to math or reasoning evaluations untested; panel selection left to future work (p. 6).
Human labels came from professional annotators judging whether the reference answer is contained in the generation; two of the five annotated datasets were triple-annotated (p. 4, pp. 11-12).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: several judges from different families pooled by vote, which is EngTrace's Layer 1 template screen (now three judges from outside the roster: Grok 4.6, MiniMax M3, MiMo-V2.5-Pro; state brief section 1); reference-based judging, as in E5, where the judge checks a milestone the gold computed; and validation of judges against human labels with chance-corrected agreement. Lacks: generated instances, gold traces, step-level or process evaluation (it judges only final QA answers and chat preferences), any STEM or engineering content (untested on math or reasoning, p. 6), and domain-expert validation (its annotators are generalist professionals judging answer containment, p. 11). It is an evaluation-method paper, not a benchmark.
notes: Batch V question: PoLL bears directly on the judge-validity half of the planned paragraph. It documents intra-model (self-preference) bias (p. 5, citing Panickssery et al. 2024 on p. 2), shows that a single judge's agreement swings with the prompt (p. 5), finds no single best judge across settings (p. 6), and validates judges against human labels with Cohen's kappa (p. 4). With the AI Tribunal reduced to the Layer 1 template screen, PoLL fits that screen better than it fitted the May Tribunal, because the screen's three judges come from families outside the roster (state brief section 1); the revised text may cite PoLL there for the disjoint-family panel. It should not cite PoLL for the evaluator: E5 and the step router use one judge (MiMo), which is the arrangement PoLL argues against, so the evaluator's validity rests on EngTrace's own expert study (X1). PoLL's self-preference evidence does support the roster rule that no judge is evaluated (D-110) and the judge-overlap check (pooled score 0.379 against 0.378 with non-suite judges; state brief section 3). Its kappas concern binary correctness of short QA answers judged by generalist annotators and say nothing about step-level engineering judgements, where EngTrace measured its judge directly (for example the router's precision 0.707 and recall 0.603 on labelled traces). The llm_judge search note lists candidates reporting correlated errors within judge panels; I have not read them, but PoLL should not be cited alone as evidence that panels remove bias. Other notes: the paper calls Cohen's kappa a 'correlation' (p. 1, p. 4); the revised text should say 'agreement'. PoLL is not best in every column: Haiku alone beats it on single-hop HotpotQA (Table 1, p. 4), and single judges match or beat it on the multi-hop sets (Bamboogle total: Haiku 0.898 against PoLL 0.896; multi-hop HotpotQA total: Command R 0.886 against 0.871; Tables 5-6, pp. 10-11), so 'outperforms a single large judge' is a claim against GPT-4 only.
